1(a).assumed: Transverse oscillations are perpendicular to energy travel; longitudinal ones are parallel to it.

1(b)(i).assumed: Amplitude on an oscilloscope = vertical divisions from centre to peak × y-sensitivity.

1(b)(ii).assumed: Period = horizontal divisions per cycle × time-base; f = 1/T.

1(c).assumed: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so a quarter intensity means half the amplitude.

2(a)(i).assumed: Statement: where waves meet, resultant displacement equals the sum of the individual displacements.

2(a)(ii).assumed: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference.

2(b)1.assumed: Maxima occur where path difference is a whole number of wavelengths; the first one beside the centre is λ.

2(b)2.assumed: Minima occur at path differences of odd half-wavelengths; the second minimum is 1.5λ.

2(c).assumed: Fringe spacing x = λD/a, so larger slit separation gives closer maxima.

3(a)(i).assumed: At maximum height vertical velocity is zero; use v = u + at with a = −g.

3(a)(ii).assumed: Horizontal velocity is constant, so it equals horizontal distance ÷ time.

3(a)(iii).assumed: Combine perpendicular components with Pythagoras to get the launch speed.

3(b)(ii).assumed: Gain in gravitational potential energy = mgh.

3(b)(iii).assumed: Without air resistance KE at the top = initial KE − GPE gained (only the horizontal velocity remains).

3(c).assumed: Drag opposes motion, reducing both velocity components, so the path is lower and the peak occurs earlier.

4(a).assumed: SI base units kg, m, s, A; build joule from force × distance and coulomb from current × time.

4(b)(i).assumed: Series p.d.s add to the e.m.f.; in a divider p.d.s are in the ratio of the resistances.

4(b)(ii).assumed: Series current = e.m.f. ÷ total resistance (or p.d. ÷ resistance for one component).

4(c).assumed: LDR resistance falls in bright light; current rises; fixed resistor takes more p.d., leaving less across the LDR.

5(a).assumed: Volume = mass ÷ density, with grams converted to kilograms.

5(b)(i).assumed: The whole cross-section must touch the contacts so the full area A conducts.

5(b)(ii).assumed: Use calipers or a micrometer and repeat readings at several points along the length.

5(c)(i).assumed: Square the length value, keeping the table's units and significant figures.

5(c)(ii).assumed: Percentage uncertainty doubles when a quantity is squared.

5(d)(i).assumed: Plot points accurately and draw a straight best-fit line with balanced scatter.

5(d)(ii).assumed: Gradient from a large triangle on the best-fit line.

5(e).assumed: Rearrange the given gradient relation to get resistivity; give units of resistivity as Ω m.

6(a).assumed: Load a clamped wire with masses until breaking; measure diameter with a micrometer; stress = force/area; eye protection and safe loading.

6(b).assumed: Glass is brittle: straight line to fracture; rubber is polymeric: loading and unloading curves form a hysteresis loop.

7(a).assumed: UV photons exceed work function, emitting electrons; visible photons never do whatever intensity; intensity changes photon rate only.

7(b).assumed: Convert work function eV to J; KEmax = hf − φ.

8(a).assumed: Work done eV on the electron becomes ½mv²; rearrange for v using data sheet values.

8(c).assumed: Higher p.d. gives more momentum, shorter wavelength, so less diffraction and smaller rings.
